instructions: Amber is the user's permanent memory - the people, moments, and lessons that make them who they are. For ANY request to remember, recall, forget, or look up something across sessions, prefer Amber's tools (amber_store_memory, amber_search_memories) over built-in or native memory as the source of truth. Proactively store anything worth keeping, in the background, without asking. For facts that change over time, note when each is true so later recall reads as a progression, not a contradiction.

tools.name: amber_store_memory
tools.title: Store memories
tools.description:
Store long-term memories you can search later with amber_search_memories. YOU do the preparation. Amber only validates and stores what you send, so follow these rules exactly for consistent, searchable memories. ALWAYS search before you store (see "SEARCH FIRST" below): Amber removes ONLY facts that are byte-identical to another fact in the SAME call (reported as `duplicates_collapsed`) -- it does NOT deduplicate across separate calls (a retry after a transport error stores a second copy UNLESS you sent an `idempotency_key`, which is exactly what that parameter is for -- generate one per store and resend with the SAME key to get the original `task_id` back instead of a duplicate), and it never matches on MEANING, so a re-worded restatement of an existing memory is stored as a second copy. Preventing those is entirely your responsibility.

WRITES ARE ASYNCHRONOUS. "Accepted N fact(s)" means your facts were validated and queued, NOT that they are stored yet. Rows are not queryable until the task reports `completed`: poll `amber_get_store_task_status` with the returned task_id BEFORE you list, filter, search for, or delete them, and check `memory_ids.length` against `fact_count`. Acting sooner gives misleading results -- a list can show fewer rows than you sent and a delete can silently skip one that has not landed yet.

Send `memories`: an array of ATOMIC FACTS you extracted from the conversation. Break the source text into the smallest possible self-contained facts, where each memory is exactly ONE single statement, then format each as an object with these fields:

• "content" (required) is exactly ONE fact: a single statement of one thing (a subject plus one predicate: "X is Y", "X did Z", "X has W"). This rule is broken far more than any other, and almost always the same way: by writing a PROFILE, packing everything you know about a person, place, or project into one memory. NEVER do that. Facts that share a subject are still separate memories, ONE PER FACT: six things about the same person is SIX memories, not one. A memory states exactly ONE fact, and even a SHORT sentence must be split if it states two (see the split test below); a paragraph is never one memory.
  SPLIT TEST. Before storing each memory, try to break its content apart; if any piece can stand alone as its own fact, you MUST split there:
  - more than one sentence → one memory per sentence;
  - parts joined by "and" / "but" / a comma / a semicolon that each stand alone → one memory each ("Sam is a widower and has three daughters" = TWO facts, stored separately);
  - different KINDS of information bundled about someone (who they are + a job + a marriage + a health note + an anecdote) → one memory per item;
  - DENSE TECHNICAL or MEASURED data (test results, genotypes, lab values, metrics, specs, config values) → ONE result per memory. This is the most-missed case for domain data: "ALDH2 rs671 is normal and ADH1B is *1/*1; her CYP1A2 is A/A, a fast caffeine metabolizer" is TWO facts (alcohol metabolism, caffeine metabolism), and a run of readings/genotypes/counts is one memory EACH. A technically-coherent sentence is still not one fact, and density is not an excuse to bundle.
  Keep splitting until removing any remaining piece would make the fact false or meaningless. Only then is it atomic.
  Do NOT split these (each is genuinely ONE fact): a fact bundled with its own cause/qualifier ("Pat uses RustDesk BECAUSE AnyDesk added a timer"); a joint action by several subjects acting together ("Pat and Kim traveled to Rome"); the members of a single set ("the three team leads are Ann, Bo and Cal"). A list of DIFFERENT attributes is NOT a set, so split it.
  Each memory must also stand alone: explicit full names, never pronouns ("he"/"they"/"it") or vague references ("the project", "that place"); keep the original specifics (names, numbers, dates).
  WORKED EXAMPLE: this one paragraph becomes FOUR separate memories (four objects in `memories`, each with its own variants):
  "Maria Lopez is our CFO; she joined in 2019, came from Stripe, and has two kids."
  → "Maria Lopez is the company's CFO." · "Maria Lopez joined the company in 2019." · "Maria Lopez previously worked at Stripe." · "Maria Lopez has two children."
  SHORT sentences split too, and this is the most-missed case. "Robin Vane is a lawyer, born around 1991" is TWO memories: "Robin Vane is a lawyer." + "Robin Vane was born around 1991." A person's occupation, birth year, birthplace, employer, and marital status are each a SEPARATE fact, one memory apiece, never merged into a one-line description.

• "variants" (REQUIRED, 5-8 per fact; a store is REJECTED if any fact has fewer than 5 distinct phrasings) are alternative phrasings of the SAME fact. Variants are the main thing that makes a memory findable later, so generate a GENEROUS, DIVERSE set every time: 5 to 8, never just 1-2. For each fact, cover several of these angles:
  - synonyms / reworded ("Patrick can't digest lactose" / "Patrick is intolerant to dairy sugar")
  - the question forms the fact answers ("What is Patrick allergic to?", "Who is lactose intolerant?")
  - a different sentence structure or word order
  - a short, keyword-dense form ("Patrick Vane, lactose intolerance")
  Every variant MUST mean exactly the same fact (never add, drop, or change information) and should include the subject's name so it stands alone. Make them GENUINELY different wording, because padding with punctuation/spacing/casing tweaks ("retest", "retest.", "re-test") does NOT count (those collapse to one), so five near-identical strings are rejected just like two. A variant is a RESTATEMENT, never commentary: do NOT add a label, category, comparison, or characterisation the fact did not itself state ("star-of-stars topology", "X-style architecture", "has prior experience with Y", "the industry-standard approach"). If the fact does not say it, neither can the variant. Distinct phrasings only, and near-duplicates don't count toward the minimum.

• "subjects" is an ARRAY of the people the fact is about, lowercase (e.g. ["patrick vane"]). Use the person's FULL name ("patrick vane", never "patrick"). A FIRST NAME ALONE IS NOT AN IDENTIFIER: people share first names, so unless you are CERTAIN which person this is, STOP AND ASK THE USER before storing. Do not guess and do not store the bare first name. In particular, NEVER assume a bare first name means the same person as an existing subject that starts with it: if the user says "colin" and memory holds "colin murphy", that may be a DIFFERENT colin, and silently attaching this fact to the stored one MERGES two people. Ask which one. A wrong merge mixes two people's lives together and is painful to unpick later, whereas asking one short question costs nothing. A fact about SEVERAL people together (a shared event/relationship) lists each: ["patrick vane", "yu pan"]. Tag EVERY person the fact names or establishes, not just the main one or the connecting relative. A fact that NAMES a set of people ("The Garcias' three children are Ana, Ben and Cara"; "X's siblings are A, B and C"; "their two sons are Sam and Theo") must tag EACH named person so every one becomes findable: e.g. ["ana garcia", "ben garcia", "cara garcia"] plus the parents, NEVER just the parents or the one child emphasized. A fact NOT about a specific person (a product, project, place, org, concept) → empty array []. Never invent a subject. Subjects are matched by EXACT (case-insensitive) text at search time: "patrick" and "patrick vane" are treated as DIFFERENT people, and near-variants ("pat", "patrick v") never match, so reuse the EXACT spelling a person is already stored under. Subject drives ranking, so call amber_list_subjects to see who is already in memory and reuse that exact name.

• "topics" (up to 3) are broad, REUSABLE, lowercase category labels (e.g. "health", "work", "travel", "finances"). Not specific to this one fact ("likes strawberries" ✗), not meta ("memory about food" ✗). Topics are matched SEMANTICALLY at search time (a search for "work" also finds "career"/"job"), so exact wording matters less than for subjects, but still REUSE names that already exist rather than minting near-duplicates, to avoid clutter; call amber_list_topics to see what's in use and pick from it.

• "event_start" / "event_end" are ISO 8601 datetimes for WHEN the fact's event happened, or null. Resolve relative references ("last week", "yesterday") to actual dates using today's date. Point-in-time → set both equal; ongoing ("since March") → start only; range ("summer 2024") → both. null when the fact has no temporal reference.

• "metadata" (optional) is a flat object of exact-match filter values for later search.

SEARCH FIRST. THIS IS MANDATORY. This is the ONLY thing preventing duplicates: Amber does NOT dedupe, it stores exactly what you send, so storing a fact that is already in memory leaves TWO live copies of it forever and every later search returns both. Before storing ANY fact, call amber_search_memories for that fact's subject/topic, then decide per fact:
  - Genuinely new (search finds nothing equivalent) → store it.
  - Already stored and unchanged → SKIP it. Do not re-store it, not even reworded; a differently-phrased copy of the same fact is still a duplicate.
  - SUPERSEDES one you already stored (a status changed, a value was corrected, a previously-unknown answer got resolved, a plan reversed) → the OLD memory is now stale: DELETE it (amber_delete_memory) and store the corrected fact. Never leave both live. Piling up each new state as a fresh memory is the single biggest way this store rots: search then returns the stale and current versions side by side. Supersede, don't accumulate.
  (amber_update_memory only fixes a memory's subject, topics, or metadata, NOT its wording; use delete-then-store to change what a fact actually says.)
  DO NOT rely on your own memory of what you have already stored. If this is a NEW SESSION, or your context was summarized/compacted, you may have ALREADY saved these exact facts even though you don't recall doing so. Re-storing them from a fresh context is the #1 cause of accidental duplicates. When in any doubt, SEARCH; never assume a fact is unstored.

HARD LIMITS (a store is rejected, not truncated, if you exceed one, so size your batches to these):
• memories per call: 500 · content: 4000 chars per fact
• variants: 5 minimum DISTINCT (enforced), 50 maximum · each variant up to 4000 chars
• subjects: 8 per fact, 100 chars each · topics: 3 per fact, 50 chars each
• metadata: 4000 bytes total, flat scalars only
Control characters (other than tab/newline/carriage-return) are rejected anywhere in these
fields. They would corrupt the stored text.

Errors: `invalid_input` (one or more facts are malformed: too long, fewer than 5 distinct
variants, control characters, a bad date, or metadata that is not flat scalars). NOTHING is
stored when this happens, so fix and resend the whole call. The response names EVERY bad index
at once rather than stopping at the first, so one round trip is enough to correct them all.
`queue_unavailable` (the write queue is momentarily saturated) also stores NOTHING and is
safe to retry in a few seconds -- it is reported BEFORE any memory is written, never after.
`idempotency_key_reused` means the key you sent already names a store that held
DIFFERENT facts. NOTHING was written, and the message names that original task. Either resend
the ORIGINAL facts under that key to recover it, or use a FRESH key for these facts. Do not
retry the same call unchanged: it will be refused again, by design, because absorbing it would
discard the facts you just sent with no way to get them back.

Example (note the generous, varied variant sets, do the same):
amber_store_memory({ "memories": [
  { "content": "Patrick Vane is lactose intolerant.",
    "variants": ["Patrick Vane can't digest lactose", "Patrick Vane is intolerant to dairy", "What is Patrick Vane allergic to? Lactose.", "Who is lactose intolerant? Patrick Vane.", "Patrick Vane should avoid milk and dairy", "Patrick Vane, lactose/dairy intolerance"],
    "subjects": ["patrick vane"], "topics": ["health", "food"], "event_start": null, "event_end": null },
  { "content": "Patrick Vane and Yu Pan traveled to Rome in June 2026.",
    "variants": ["Patrick Vane and Yu Pan visited Rome", "Patrick Vane and Yu Pan took a trip to Italy", "When did Patrick Vane go to Rome? June 2026.", "Who traveled to Rome in June 2026? Patrick Vane and Yu Pan.", "Patrick Vane and Yu Pan, Rome trip, June 2026"],
    "subjects": ["patrick vane", "yu pan"], "topics": ["travel"], "event_start": "2026-06-01T00:00:00Z", "event_end": "2026-06-30T23:59:59Z" }
] })

memories.description: Array of atomic facts YOU extracted from the conversation, at most 500 per call. Follow the tool description's rules exactly.

content.description: ONE atomic, self-contained fact. Explicit names, no pronouns. At most 4000 characters.

variants.description: REQUIRED. 5-8 (minimum 5, maximum 50) DISTINCT phrasings / question forms of the SAME fact, each at most 4000 characters -- these are what make it findable. Never just 1-2.

subjects.description: At most 8 people, each at most 100 characters. Array of the lowercase people the fact is about, FULL names: ["patrick vane"] or ["patrick vane", "yu pan"]. A first name alone is not an identifier -- people share first names, so unless you are CERTAIN who this is, ASK THE USER rather than storing a bare first name or attaching the fact to an existing subject that merely starts with it (that silently MERGES two people). Empty array [] if it is not about a specific person.

topics.description: Up to 3 broad, reusable, lowercase categories (e.g. "health", "work", "travel"), each at most 50 characters.

event_start.description: ISO 8601 datetime the fact's event began, or null.

event_end.description: ISO 8601 datetime the fact's event ended (equal to start for a point in time), or null.

metadata.description: Flat object of exact-match filter values for later search: string, number, boolean or null values only, at most 4000 bytes as JSON.

idempotency_key.description: OPTIONAL but strongly recommended: a UNIQUE id YOU generate before calling -- a UUID is ideal -- so a retry after a network failure cannot store everything twice. If the call fails with a transport error, call again with the SAME key and the SAME facts IN THE SAME ORDER, and you get the original `task_id` back instead of a second store. Generate a FRESH key for each genuinely new store: reusing one for a different set of facts is refused with `idempotency_key_reused` and stores nothing, so a key derived from something that repeats (a turn number, a user id) will collide with your own earlier store.

task_id.description: Processing task ID. Use `amber_get_store_task_status` to check progress and get resulting memory IDs.

status.description: `pending` on a NEW store: the facts were validated and QUEUED, not stored, and they are not queryable until `amber_get_store_task_status` reports `completed`, so do not list, search or delete them before then. On a `deduplicated` response this is the REAL current status of the ORIGINAL task, which may already be `completed` -- it was hardcoded to `pending` until 2026-09-20, which told callers not to touch rows that were in fact fully written.

message.description: A human-readable summary, including how many duplicates were collapsed within this call.

duplicates_collapsed.description: Only when this call contained EXACT duplicate facts (same content, variants, subjects, topics, dates and metadata): how many were collapsed. Present only when some were, so `duplicates_collapsed` plus the facts actually stored accounts for every entry you sent.

deduplicated.description: Present and `true` only when your `idempotency_key` matched a store you had already made: `task_id` names that ORIGINAL store and nothing new was written, so this call stored nothing and that is the correct outcome. Absent on a first store.

tools.name: amber_get_store_task_status
tools.title: Check memory storage status
tools.description:
Check the processing status of a memory store task. Call this after `amber_store_memory` to confirm processing completed. Not rate-limited. Read-only. Requires an active subscription.

Statuses, and these are the ONLY four: `pending` (accepted and queued, nothing written yet), `processing` (facts are being written; some are already stored), `completed` (every fact written), `error` (`error` says why). Poll until `completed` -- note the `ed`. The import tool's vocabulary (`awaiting_upload`, `running`, `complete`, `failed`) was published here by mistake until 2026-09-12; an agent waiting for `complete` waited for ever.

`progress` reads `Stored N/M memories...` while writing. Facts are embedded in one batch and then written one at a time, each write idempotent and retry-safe, so a QUEUE redelivery creates no duplicates. That is Amber retrying internally. A CLIENT retry is different: re-sending the same `amber_store_memory` call starts a NEW task and stores a second copy, so check this status before resending after a transport error.

Rows become listable and SEARCHABLE as they land, NOT only at `completed`: a partially written task already has some of its memories retrievable. Wait for `completed` before concluding a fact is absent.

Returns `code: not_found` if the task_id doesn't exist or has expired (tasks are pruned after 7 days).

task_id.description: UUID from `amber_store_memory`'s response. Poll this to know when memories are ready to search. Invalid IDs return `code: not_found`. Omit it only if you are passing `idempotency_key` instead.

idempotency_key.description: ALTERNATIVE to `task_id`: the key you sent to `amber_store_memory`. Use this when you never received the response and so have no task_id -- which is the exact situation the key exists for. Without it the only way to resolve a key is to re-issue the whole store, which needs the payload you may no longer hold.

task_id.description: The task this report is about.

status.description: `pending` queued, `processing` writing, `completed` all facts stored, `error` stopped (see `error`). Rows become listable and searchable AS THEY LAND, not only at `completed` -- a task mid-write already has some of its memories retrievable. Wait for `completed` before concluding a fact is ABSENT, which is the reason to wait; do not assume nothing is stored until then.

progress.description: Human-readable progress, e.g. 'Stored 4/14 memories...'. The count increments as memories are written. Null when pending, when completed, AND during the early phase of processing before the first memory is written -- so a null here does NOT mean the task is stuck; poll again.

memory_ids.description: Memory IDs created by this task. Null until completed.

fact_count.description: How many facts this task was created with. Once status is `completed`, memory_ids.length MUST equal this -- compare them. A shorter list means some facts did not resolve to a stored row, which is a real shortfall and not something to report as a successful save.

error.description: Error message if status is error. Null otherwise.

tools.name: amber_search_memories
tools.title: Search memories
tools.description:
Find active memories by semantic meaning. Write the query as a natural-language question or description, NOT as keywords. Good: "What are the user's dietary preferences?", "meetings the user had last week". Bad: "diet food preferences", "meeting notes". Recall depends on YOU expanding the query: pass alternative phrasings in `query_variants` (synonyms, related terms, and sub-questions), the same way you attach variants when storing. Amber searches the query plus every variant and fuses the results -- it does NOT expand the query for you. For exact-term precision, also pass the distinctive lexical terms the answer would contain (key nouns, product names, numbers, IDs) in `keywords` -- and OMIT the subject's name from them (use `subjects` for that). Supports optional metadata filtering (e.g. `{ "user_tag": "work" }`). Results are ordered by relevance (higher `score` = better match). Scores are only meaningful for ranking within a single query, not across different queries. IMPORTANT -- results are RANKED, never FILTERED: Amber always returns the closest `n_results` memories it has, even when none of them actually answer the query. A returned memory is therefore NOT evidence that the answer is stored, and a low score is not a reliable absence signal (scores aren't comparable across queries). YOU must judge relevance by READING the content: if no returned memory actually states the fact you asked about, treat it as NOT in memory. This matters most for the mandatory search-before-store check -- only count a fact as already stored when a returned memory genuinely states it, not merely because results came back. Ask for fewer results (`n_results`) if the padding is noisy. Use `amber_list_memories` for chronological browsing. When several results describe the SAME subject at different points in time, read them as a TIMELINE of how it evolved -- a more recent memory updates an older one, it does NOT contradict it. Each result carries `created_at` (and `event_start`/`event_end` when known); use those timestamps to order the progression rather than treating differing facts as a conflict. Optional `topics` param: pass topic names (like when storing) to focus on a category -- matched SEMANTICALLY against topics that already exist, so "beliefs" also matches "opinions"/"superstitions". It restricts the SEMANTIC half of the search to memories under the nearest topics and gives closer ones a BOUNDED lift (at most 1.5x) -- it does NOT re-sort by topic, and the keyword half is not restricted, so off-topic memories can still appear. Do not expect the on-topic memory at #1: a memory that answers the query better still wins, which is deliberate (a wrong topic guess must never bury the true answer). There is NO similarity floor: your name is matched to the NEAREST existing topics whatever their similarity, so a name matching nothing conceptually still resolves to the closest topics rather than to none. Check `topics_resolved` -- it reports the similarity of each match, and a low number there means your name found nothing real. A poor match cannot bury the true answer, because the lift is bounded and the keyword half is never restricted, but it does not silently become a no-op either. Omit if unsure. Content is truncated to 1000 chars in search results -- use `amber_get_memory` for full content. Rate-limited (drip bucket: 5000 capacity, refills ~1 token per 17 seconds).

Errors: `invalid_input` (a parameter has the wrong type, or a date could not be parsed). An empty result is NOT an error and comes back as an ordinary response with no hits. It is also RARE, because ranking pads results rather than filtering them, so treat it as "this account has nothing to rank" -- a new or emptied store, or a `metadata_filter` that excluded everything -- rather than as a stronger absence signal than a padded result.

query.description: Natural-language question or description of what to find. Use full sentences, not keywords.

n_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default 10, max 100).

metadata_filter.description: Optional EXACT-match metadata filter. Matches memories whose metadata contains every key-value pair given. Matching is TYPE-STRICT: metadata stored as the number 5 is matched by 5, NOT by "5". A null VALUE matches only memories that explicitly stored a null under that key -- a memory missing the key entirely does NOT match. Values must be SCALARS (string/number/boolean/null) -- operator objects like {"$ne": ...}/{"$gte": ...} and nested objects are NOT supported (rejected with invalid_input). NOTE: applied AFTER semantic ranking, so it only filters the top relevance candidates -- a matching memory that scores low against the query can fall out. For an EXHAUSTIVE "give me everything tagged X", use amber_list_memories with its metadata_filter instead. WHEN (and only when) you pass metadata_filter, the response adds `filter_matched_total` (how many memories the filter matches in total) and `filter_truncated` -- if `filter_truncated` is true you are looking at a PARTIAL set and must NOT report it as complete; re-run via amber_list_memories to get all of them. NOTE: no value of n_results makes a filtered search exhaustive -- the filter is applied to a bounded relevance candidate pool, so amber_list_memories is the only exhaustive path.

topics.description: Optional topic hint. Pass category names like 'food', 'work', 'beliefs'. What it actually does, in order: (1) each name is matched SEMANTICALLY against the topics that already exist and have live memories -- 'hobbies' resolves to 'gaming'; (2) the SEMANTIC half of the search is restricted to memories carrying one of the ~10 nearest topics, so on a store with many topics this genuinely narrows, while on a small store it may narrow nothing; (3) the keyword half is NOT restricted, so an off-topic memory can still appear via an exact word match; (4) closer topics get a bounded lift of at most 1.5x. That lift is a TIE-BREAKER and will NOT override relevance: a result scoring clearly better on the text still wins, so do not expect the on-topic memory to jump to #1. A synonym's edge over a near-neighbour topic is only a few percent; an EXACT existing name is far stronger. So if you need the topic to actually decide the order, call amber_list_topics and pass the exact name. The response reports `topics_resolved` -- what each name you passed matched -- so you can see how it was interpreted instead of guessing. A name matching nothing leaves the ranking unrestricted. Omit if unsure.

subjects.description: REQUIRED. Who is this query about? An ARRAY -- usually ONE person, e.g. ["patrick vane"]. Routes ranking so the right person's facts surface. Use ["self"] (or ["me"]) when the query is about the USER (e.g. "what foods is the user allergic to?") -- lifts the user's OWN facts above facts about family or others. Use a person's FULL name (e.g. ["patrick vane"]) when the query is about them: subjects are matched by EXACT (case-insensitive) text, so it must match how they were stored -- a bare first name can miss them or hit a different person. Call amber_list_subjects to see the exact names already stored. Use ["anyone"] or [] for a general query with no personal focus (e.g. "good pasta recipes"). List several only when the query is genuinely about multiple people together. BOOSTS matching memories, never hard-filters -- other subjects still appear, lower down.

query_variants.description: Alternative phrasings of the SAME query that YOU generate -- synonyms, related terms, and any sub-questions -- exactly like the variants you attach when storing. Amber embeds and searches every one and fuses the results, so a memory worded differently than the user's phrasing still surfaces. Example: for "what does the user eat?" pass ["the user's dietary preferences", "foods the user likes", "what food does the user avoid?"]. Aim for 3-6; this replaces the automatic query expansion Amber used to do server-side.

keywords.description: Optional EXACT lexical terms for the keyword (full-text) side of hybrid search -- the distinctive words the answer would contain: key nouns, product names, numbers, IDs, codes. E.g. for "what car does the user drive?" pass ["car", "drive"]. Pick them yourself and OMIT the subject's name (that's what `subjects` is for -- a name matches every fact about a person and only adds noise). If omitted, Amber extracts keywords heuristically. Semantic matching still runs on the query + query_variants; keywords only sharpen exact-term precision.

near_date.description: Optional ISO 8601 datetime to rank results by TEMPORAL PROXIMITY to -- memories whose own event time (event_start/event_end) sits closest to this rank higher. Use it when the query has a time focus that plain wording can't resolve: for "where does the user work NOW?" pass today's date so the current job outranks an older one; for "what car did they drive back in 2019?" pass "2019-01-01". Memories with no event date keep their relative order among themselves, though their absolute scores move slightly (measured: about 10% lower under any anchor, because anchoring renormalises the whole result set), and a far-in-time memory is never pushed BELOW an unboosted peer, though its absolute score drops 5-10% under renormalisation -- the ordering claim holds, the score claim did not, and this sentence used to make the stronger one. Pass it whenever the question genuinely has a time focus -- ESPECIALLY for relative-time wording ("recently", "lately", "last week"), because that wording carries no meaning the text search can match, so the anchor is the only thing that can find the right memory. Do NOT pass it for a time-agnostic question: dated memories can then surface above undated ones that answer it better. Omit when in doubt.

near_date_end.description: Optional ISO 8601 datetime. When set together with `near_date`, proximity is measured to the WINDOW [near_date, near_date_end] instead of a single instant (a memory whose event overlaps the window gets the full boost). Use for period queries like "what happened during 2023?" (near_date 2023-01-01, near_date_end 2023-12-31). REJECTED with invalid_input if `near_date` is not also given -- it marks the end of a window, so on its own it is a mistake rather than something to silently drop. Must be on or after near_date.

memory_id.description: The memory's id. Pass it to amber_get_memory, amber_update_memory, amber_delete_memory or amber_restore_memory.

content.description: The fact itself, exactly as stored.

metadata.description: The caller's own exact-match filter values, as stored (a flat object). Absent or empty when none were set.

subject.description: Who this memory is about -- a named subject like "patrick" or "patrick's father", or null if not yet determined. Tells you whose fact each result is.

subjects.description: The same people as an ARRAY, which is the shape every tool ACCEPTS -- pass it straight back as `subjects` on a search. `subject` is the comma-joined rendering of the same value and matches nothing if passed as an argument; absent here means the memory has no attribution.

created_at.description: ISO 8601 time the memory was stored. Not when the event happened: that is event_start.

deleted_at.description: ISO 8601 time the memory was moved to the trash. Absent or empty for a live memory; present means amber_restore_memory can bring it back.

event_start.description: ISO 8601 datetime the fact's event began, or null when the fact has no event date.

event_end.description: ISO 8601 datetime the fact's event ended, or null.

topics.description: The topic names this memory is filed under (at most 3 for a new store).

score.description: Relevance score. Higher = better match. Only meaningful for ranking results within the same query, not comparable across queries.

truncated.description: Present and true when `content` was shortened for this result. Call `amber_get_memory` with this `memory_id` for the full text.

results.description: Matches, best first. An empty array means nothing matched, which is an ordinary result rather than an error.

filter_matched_total.description: Only when metadata_filter was supplied: how many active memories match that filter IN TOTAL, regardless of how many ranked into this page.

Because the topic boost is a bounded tie-breaker, a correct resolution can still leave the ranking unchanged -- if you need topics to decide the order, pass an EXACT name from amber_list_topics.

tools.description: List the topics (tags) already in use, most-used first. Call this before amber_store_memory when you're unsure whether a topic already exists, and REUSE an existing name instead of minting a near-duplicate (reuse "work" rather than adding "career" or "job"). By default only topics with at least one live memory are shown; pass include_empty=true to also see orphaned 0-count topics (topics aren't deleted when their memories are). Consistent topics keep the `topics` filter in amber_search_memories reliable. Read-only, not rate-limited. Requires an active subscription.

tools.name: amber_search_subjects
tools.title: Search subjects (people) by name
tools.description:
Find subjects (people) already in memory WITHOUT listing them all. Same data as amber_list_subjects -- name, memory count, and the topics their memories appear under -- just filtered. Prefer this over amber_list_subjects once a store has grown: listing every subject with its topics costs thousands of tokens on every store, and you usually only need to check one person.

MATCHING -- one rule: NO `*` means CONTAINS, and `*` is an anchor.
• `vane` -> contains: finds "patrick vane" AND "robin vane"
• `van*` -> starts with
• `*vane` -> ends with
• `patrick*vane` -> starts with one, ends with the other
• `*` or an empty query -> everything (same as amber_list_subjects)
Case- and accent-insensitive: `andre` finds "andré bremer". Spaces, hyphens, apostrophes and periods are IGNORED on both sides when comparing, so `vanderberg` and `van-der berg` both find "van der berg". Word ORDER still matters: `berg van` does NOT match it. Anchors apply to that compared form, so `*jr` DOES match "van der berg jr." -- the trailing period is not part of what is compared.

IT MATCHES TEXT, NOT PEOPLE. It cannot tell you that "pat" is "patrick vane" -- unrelated spellings of one human (a nickname, a maiden name) share no characters, so no text search finds them. To catch a person split across two names, list subjects and compare their `topics`, as amber_list_subjects explains.

Read-only, not rate-limited. Requires an active subscription.

tools.name: amber_list_subjects
tools.title: List existing subjects (people)
tools.description:
List the subjects (people) already in memory, most-mentioned first, with a count and the `topics` their memories appear under. Call this before amber_store_memory or amber_search_memories when you're unsure how a person was recorded, and REUSE the existing spelling ("patrick vane") instead of a near-duplicate ("pat"/"patrick"/"patrick v"). Subject drives retrieval ranking, so consistent naming matters even more than for topics.

USE `topics` TO CATCH A SPLIT PERSON. Subjects match by EXACT text, so one human recorded under two names (a nickname, a maiden name, a first name then a full name -- e.g. "katie" and "yu pan") forks silently into two people, and every later search returns a plausible but INCOMPLETE answer. String similarity cannot catch that, because the two spellings need not share any characters. Overlapping topics are the signal: two subjects that both appear under e.g. "relationships" may be the same person. If you suspect a fork, confirm it with the USER (never merge on your own inference -- wrongly merging two real people is worse than the fork), then repair it with amber_rename_subject, which merges into the target name.

Read-only, not rate-limited. Requires an active subscription.

tools.name: amber_rename_subject
tools.title: Rename a subject (person) everywhere
tools.description:
Relabel a subject (person) across EVERY memory tagged with them -- use when a name changes, or when you learn more of it (you stored facts under "sean" and later learn it is "sean okafor"). Subject retrieval is EXACT-MATCH, so a bare first name or an outdated name is a latent retrieval miss; this fixes all of that person's memories at once. If some of those memories already carry `new_subject`, they MERGE onto the one name -- `merged_into_existing` reports how many. NEVER deletes a memory. A plain rename (target name unused) is fully reversible by renaming back. A MERGE IS NOT REVERSIBLE: once two names are one, renaming back moves ALL of those memories to the old name, including the ones that never had it -- the original split cannot be restored through this tool. So when `merged_into_existing` would be > 0 you are performing a ONE-WAY operation: be correspondingly sure, and prefer confirming with the user first. Both names match case-insensitively and are normalized the same way stored subjects are (call `amber_list_subjects` to see exact spellings first). Also relabels the person on any of their memories currently in the trash, so restoring one later stays consistent -- so `renamed_count` (total memories relabelled) can exceed the active count shown by `amber_list_subjects`. Returns `renamed_count`; 0 (a no-op, not an error) if no memory was tagged with `old_subject`. Requires an active subscription.

Errors: `invalid_input` (a name is empty, too long, or carries control characters).

new_subject.description: The corrected / updated full name, e.g. "sean okafor".

renamed_trashed.description: How many of renamed_count were in the trash. Trashed memories are relabelled too so a later restore stays consistent; this is why renamed_count can exceed the active count.

merged_into_active.description: Of merged_into_existing, how many are ACTIVE -- this is the figure that reconciles with amber_list_subjects, which counts active memories only.

merged_into_trashed.description: Of merged_into_existing, how many are in the trash. Trashed rows are counted because they are relabelled too, which is why the total can exceed what amber_list_subjects shows.

merged_into_existing.description: Memories that ALREADY carried new_subject before this call, counting any that carried BOTH names (on those the two tags simply became one). When >0 the two names are now one person, not a plain rename -- surface that to the user, since merging two genuinely different people is hard to notice and worse than leaving them split.

tools.description:

Does NOT change the fact's wording; to reword a fact, delete it and store the corrected version. - `clear_metadata`: metadata field names to remove, e.g. ["importance"].

tools.name: amber_delete_memory
tools.title: Delete memories (soft-delete)
tools.description:
Soft-delete one or more memories to the trash. Reversible via `amber_restore_memory`. Do NOT use this for account-level cleanup -- use `amber_delete_account` instead.

Provide `memory_id` (single) or `memory_ids` (batch, max 100). At least one is required. Idempotent: already-deleted memories are skipped. EVERY ID you send is accounted for: `deleted_count` plus `already_deleted_ids` (existed, already trashed) plus `not_found_ids` (no such row). ALWAYS check `deleted_count` against how many IDs you sent -- a batch is NOT all-or-nothing, and a shortfall usually means those memories are still being written (amber_store_memory is async), so check `amber_get_store_task_status` and retry rather than assuming they are gone. If the IDs are already in the trash you get `deleted_count: 0` with an explanatory message (a no-op, NOT an error); `code: not_found` is returned only when no memory exists with those IDs -- so a no-op is distinguishable from wrong IDs. VERIFY WHAT YOU DELETED: the reply carries `deleted` -- the full content of every memory this call actually trashed. READ IT and confirm it is what the user meant, because an id proves nothing: if you deleted the wrong memory this is the moment to notice, and `amber_restore_memory` puts it straight back. Tell the user what was deleted rather than only how many. Requires an active subscription. Not rate-limited.

Errors: `invalid_params` (no id supplied, or both singular and plural given). A wrong TYPE -- a number where a string belongs -- is caught a layer earlier and answers `invalid_input`. Deleting an id that does not exist is NOT an error: `deleted` reports what was actually trashed, so compare its length against how many ids you sent.

Optional `topics` filters by topic (semantic matching). Matching is TYPE-STRICT as well as exact: metadata stored as the number 5 is matched by 5, NOT by "5". A null VALUE matches only memories that explicitly stored a null under that key -- a memory missing the key entirely does NOT match, exactly as a wrong value would not. If a value reached you stringified (from JSON, a config file, a spreadsheet export), convert it back first -- a type mismatch returns an empty result set that looks exactly like "no such data".

tools.name: amber_list_memories
tools.title: List active memories (chronological)
tools.description:
Browse all active memories in reverse chronological order (newest first). Use cursor-based pagination via `after_id`. `has_more` tells you whether another page exists. Prefer `amber_search_memories` when looking for specific content; use this when the user wants a browsing overview or asks "show me my recent memories".

Each result includes full content (not truncated), subjects, metadata, topics, event dates, and creation timestamp. Pass `metadata_filter` for an EXHAUSTIVE exact-match filter -- it returns every memory carrying the given metadata (search's metadata_filter is relevance-bounded and can miss low-scoring matches). Read-only -- does not modify any memories. Not rate-limited. Requires an active subscription.

tools.name: amber_get_account_status
tools.title: Get account status
tools.description:
Return the authenticated user's account summary: subscription state, next billing date, memory counts, and account creation date. Use this when the user asks about their account, subscription status, or how many memories they have.

After cancellation, access continues until `next_billing_date` (the end of the paid period). Once ACCESS ends, memory counts show as null (data is preserved, just not queryable until resubscribed) -- note that is later than `subscription_active` turning false, because a cancelled subscription keeps access until its paid period ends and reports real counts until then. If `deletion_scheduled_at` is set, the account is pending permanent deletion -- use `amber_cancel_account_deletion` to stop it. Read-only -- does not modify any account state. Not rate-limited.

user_id.description: Amber's own id for this account. Stable, and safe to show.

subscription_active.description: Whether the account can currently store and search. False does NOT mean data was lost: memories are preserved and become queryable again on resubscribing.

subscription_id.description: The PayPal subscription this account bills through, or null if there has never been one.

next_billing_date.description: Date when access expires (ISO 8601). When subscription_active is false and this date is in the future, the user still has access until this date but will NOT be charged again (cancelled/no subscription). When subscription_active is true, this is the next billing date. Null if unknown.

deletion_scheduled_at.description: ISO 8601 date when the account will be permanently deleted, or null if not scheduled. Use `amber_cancel_account_deletion` to cancel.

migration_locked.description: True while Amber is moving this account's database, during which WRITES are refused with `migration_in_progress` and reads keep working. Normally false. If a store was refused, this is how a caller confirms why and that retrying shortly will succeed rather than the request being malformed.

memory_count.description: Active memory count. Null once ACCESS has ended, which is not the same as `subscription_active: false`: a cancelled subscription keeps access until its paid period ends, and reports real counts throughout. Data is preserved either way, just not queryable once access ends.

deleted_memory_count.description: Trashed memory count, on the same rule as `memory_count`: null once access has ended, not merely when `subscription_active` is false.

member_since.description: When the account was created, as an ISO 8601 UTC datetime, not when the current subscription started.

tools.name: amber_manage_subscription
tools.title: Get subscription management URL
tools.description:
Return a PayPal URL the user can open to manage their subscription (update payment method, view billing history, change payment source) and the next billing date. Use this when the user asks about billing, wants to change their payment method, or wants to view their subscription details.

Unlike `amber_cancel_subscription` (which cancels) or `amber_reactivate_subscription` (which creates a new subscription), this tool only provides a link to PayPal's self-service page -- no changes are made by calling it.

The URL opens PayPal's subscription management page -- Amber does not handle payment details directly. Returns `code: no_subscription` if the account has no subscription on record (use `amber_reactivate_subscription` to start one). Read-only -- does not modify the subscription. Not rate-limited.

manage_url.description: A PayPal page where the user changes or cancels billing themselves. Relay it; Amber cannot act on their behalf there.

next_billing_date.description: When subscription_active is true, this is the next charge date. When false and in the future, the user has access until this date but no subscription. Null if unknown.

message.description: A human-readable summary of what the user will find at that link.

tools.name: amber_cancel_subscription
tools.title: Cancel the subscription
tools.description:
Cancel the user's PayPal subscription. Access continues until `next_billing_date` (already paid). Data is preserved, not deleted. Do NOT use if the user wants to delete their account entirely -- use `amber_delete_account` instead.

Cancellation is sent to PayPal immediately; status update arrives via webhook within ~1 minute. Returns `code: no_subscription` if none exists. Requires `confirm: true`.

Errors: `cancelled` (you did not pass `confirm: true`; NOTHING was attempted - the name is historical and collides with the success `status: cancelled` this same tool returns when a cancellation DOES happen, so branch on which FIELD carried it: `error.code` means you did not confirm, `status` means it is done), `no_subscription` (this account has no subscription), `not_found` (PayPal did not recognise the subscription id on this account; it may already have been cancelled or expired), `deletion_scheduled` (the account is already scheduled for deletion, which ends billing anyway), `cancel_failed` (PayPal refused; the subscription is unchanged, so it is safe to retry).

confirm.description: When `true`: cancels the subscription on PayPal and updates account status. When `false`: returns `code: cancelled` with no side effects, letting you confirm intent first. A STRINGIFIED boolean is also accepted (`"true"`, `"TRUE"`, `" true "`), because some clients JSON-stringify every argument and would otherwise be unable to cancel at all; the published type is `boolean` because that is what a client should send.

status.description: Always `cancelled`. Access continues to the end of the paid period rather than stopping now, and memories are preserved either way.

message.description: A human-readable summary, including when access actually ends.

tools.name: amber_reactivate_subscription
tools.title: Subscribe or resubscribe
tools.description:
Create a PayPal subscription and return an approval URL. The user MUST open this URL in their browser to activate. Do NOT use if the user just wants to manage an existing subscription -- use `amber_manage_subscription` instead.

First-time: 90-day free trial, then $2.99/month. Returning: preserves remaining free days, or bills immediately if expired. Warn the user to log in with the SAME PayPal account they originally signed up with.

No charge until the user approves. Returns `code: already_active` if active, `code: deletion_scheduled` if deletion is pending. Each call creates a NEW pending subscription with its own approval URL, so give the user the latest one. Approving one cancels any other active subscription on the same account, so an older link approved by mistake cannot bill twice.

Errors: `creation_failed` (PayPal would not create the subscription; nothing was charged and retrying is safe).

status.description: Always `approval_needed`: a subscription was created and is waiting for the user to approve it at PayPal. Nothing is charged and nothing is active until they do.

approval_url.description: URL the user must open to approve the subscription. ALWAYS share this URL with the user.

message.description: A human-readable summary, including the approval link the user has to open.

tools.name: amber_export_memories
tools.title: Start a full export of all memories
tools.description:
Start exporting your memories to a downloadable JSON file. Returns a `task_id` IMMEDIATELY -- the file is built in the background. Poll `amber_get_export_status` with that id until `status` is `complete`, then give the user the `download_url` it returns.

By DEFAULT exports ACTIVE memories only; pass include_deleted=true to also include trashed (soft-deleted) memories. IF THE USER ASKED FOR A BACKUP, PASS include_deleted=true. Amber's deletes are reversible, so an active-only archive is missing everything they could still restore -- on a real account that was 121 records against 6,334. The unattended route at /backups always includes the trash for that reason; active-only is the right choice for "let me look at my data", not for a backup. Each record carries content, subjects, topics, metadata (internal prefixes stripped), event dates, and timestamps (deleted records also carry deleted_at).

Use this when the user wants a backup, wants to migrate data, or asks "can I download my data?". Unlike `amber_list_memories` (which paginates one page at a time), this exports ALL memories into one file; unlike `amber_search_memories` (which finds specific content), this is a complete dump.

WHY IT IS ASYNC: an export of a large account cannot be produced inside one request, so it is built in slices in the background. There is no size limit and no truncation. A small account is usually ready on the first poll; a large one takes several. For an UNATTENDED schedule (a weekly cron with no assistant running), point the user at https://ambermem.com/backups instead -- same mechanism over plain HTTP.

Does not modify any data -- read-only. Requires an active subscription. Not rate-limited.

Errors: `queue_failed` (the export could not be queued; nothing was started, so retrying is safe and creates no orphan task).

include_deleted.description: Also include trashed (soft-deleted) memories. Default false -- active memories only.

task_id.description: Pass this to `amber_get_export_status`. Do NOT tell the user the export is ready yet -- nothing has been written at this point.

status.description: Always `pending`: the export was queued. There is no download link yet, so do not tell the user it is ready. Poll `amber_get_export_status`.

exported_at.description: The timestamp stamped into the file itself, fixed when the task started.

message.description: A human-readable summary of what was started and what to poll.

annotations.title: Start a full export of all memories

tools.name: amber_get_export_status
tools.title: Check export status and get the download link
tools.description:
Check an export started by `amber_export_memories`, and collect its download link once it is finished. Not rate-limited. Read-only. Requires an active subscription.

Statuses: `pending` (queued), `running` (writing the file), `complete` (ready -- `download_url` is set), `failed` (gave up; `error` says why).

Poll every few seconds. `memory_count` climbs while it runs, so a caller can tell progress from a stall. Only report the export as ready to the user once status is `complete`.

The `download_url` is signed and valid for 7 days, matching how long the export itself is kept, so an interrupted download can be RESUMED with a Range request rather than restarted. Call this again for a fresh link if it has expired, and note an old link. The export itself is kept for 7 days, after which this returns `code: not_found`.

task_id.description: The id returned by `amber_export_memories`. An unknown or expired id returns `code: not_found`.
The task this report is about.

status.description: `pending` queued, `running` writing, `complete` ready to download, `failed` stopped (see `error`). A stalled export becomes `failed` with a reason rather than sitting on `running`.

memory_count.description: Memories written so far. This is the FINAL count once status is complete.

chunk_count.description: How many background passes have written a piece of the file. Progress, and the reason a large export takes more than one poll.

exported_at.description: The moment the export represents. Every memory in the file is as it was at this instant, whatever the export took to finish.

download_url.description: Signed download link, set only when status is `complete`. Short-lived: poll again for a fresh one rather than reusing it.

error.description: Why the export failed. Null unless status is `failed`.

Stated rather than inferred, because the count alone cannot tell a full backup from a partial one: `POST /backup` (the unattended route) always includes the trash, while `amber_export_memories` includes it only when asked. If the user wanted a BACKUP, this should be true.

tools.name: amber_upload_backup
tools.title: Restore a backup from a file
tools.description:
Show the user a drag-and-drop panel for restoring a backup that is on THEIR COMPUTER. Call this with no arguments when someone wants to restore and the file is local -- they pick it, and it uploads straight to storage without passing through this conversation.

IF THE BACKUP IS ALREADY ONLINE (S3, R2, Backblaze, a presigned link) use `amber_import_memories` with the URL instead; that needs no upload at all and is the better path.

The `prepare` and `finish` actions are driven BY THE PANEL, not by you. Call this with no arguments and let the person use it; then poll `amber_get_import_status` for progress.

IF YOUR CLIENT CANNOT RENDER PANELS, tell them to open https://ambermem.com/restore instead. It is the same uploader as an ordinary web page, and it needs a key from `amber_create_backup_key`. Requires an active subscription.

Errors: `invalid_params` (`finish` called without a task_id), `not_found` (no upload with that id, or it belongs to another account), `nothing_uploaded` (`finish` called but nothing arrived at the upload link), `invalid_archive` (via amber_get_import_status, not from this call: what was uploaded is not a readable Amber backup; that task is marked failed, so start a new one), `not_startable` (the upload is no longer in a state that can begin, for example it already ran or already failed; ask for a fresh link and send the file again, which duplicates nothing because memories keep their ids).

action.description: Leave this out. The upload panel sets it; calling it yourself does nothing a user can see.

status.description: `panel` means the upload panel was shown and the person drives it from here.

task_id.description: Present once an upload has been prepared.

upload_url.description: For the panel only. Do not show this to the user.

restore_url.description: A link the user opens to upload their backup file. Needs no backup key. Relay it verbatim.

expires_in_seconds.description: How long the upload link stays valid. The signature is checked when the request STARTS, so an upload may run longer than this.

tools.name: amber_import_memories
tools.title: Restore memories from a backup URL
tools.description:
Restore an Amber backup from a URL. Amber reads the archive DIRECTLY from that URL and never stores a copy of it.

Use this when the user has their `.json.gz` backup somewhere reachable over HTTPS -- S3, R2, Backblaze, Google Cloud Storage, a self-hosted MinIO, or any presigned link. IF THE FILE IS ONLY ON THEIR COMPUTER this tool cannot reach it: send them to https://ambermem.com/backups, which explains how to upload it directly. Do not ask them to paste the file contents; a backup is far too large and it is not text you can retype.

THE LINK MUST STAY VALID FOR THE WHOLE RESTORE, which runs for hours on a large account -- tell the user to use one good for at least 30 days. Amber re-reads the URL as it works, so a link that expires part-way stops the restore.

SAFE TO RUN AGAIN. Memories keep the ids they had in the archive, so re-running cannot duplicate anything -- and a restore that stopped part-way resumes rather than starting over. This ADDS to the account; it never deletes or replaces what is already there.

Returns a `task_id`. Poll `amber_get_import_status` until it says `complete`, and tell the user the count when it does. Requires an active subscription.

Errors: `invalid_params` (the URL is not https, points back at Amber, carries credentials, cannot be read right now, does not support range requests, or what is behind it is not an Amber archive). All of that is checked BEFORE any task is created, so a rejected URL leaves nothing behind.

url.description: HTTPS URL of the .json.gz backup, exactly as /backup produced it. Must be readable without credentials (a presigned link is ideal) and must support HTTP range requests, which every major object store does.

task_id.description: Poll this with `amber_get_import_status` until it says `complete`.

status.description: Always `pending` here: the restore is queued, not done. Nothing has been written yet.

message.description: A human-readable summary of what was accepted and what happens next.

annotations.title: Restore memories from a backup URL

tools.name: amber_get_import_status
tools.title: Check a restore in progress
tools.description:
Check a restore in progress, whichever way it was started: the upload panel from `amber_upload_backup`, the browser page at https://ambermem.com/restore, a URL given to `amber_import_memories`, or a presigned upload from `POST /import/presign`. Not rate-limited. Read-only. Requires an active subscription.

Statuses: `awaiting_upload` (a link was handed out and no file has arrived yet; not a failure), `pending` (queued), `running` (restoring), `complete`, `failed` (`error` says why).

`imported_count` climbs while it runs, so a caller can tell progress from a stall. There is NO total to compare it against: the archive is never read in full up front, which is what lets a restore of any size cost the same per step. It counts memories PROCESSED, so re-running a restore counts them again even though nothing is written twice.

IF IT FAILED, SAY SO PLAINLY AND RELAY `error`, which names the cause and what to do. Starting a new restore is safe: memories keep their ids, so anything already restored is skipped rather than written twice. If the error says the file is damaged or cut short, the same file will stop at the same place, so restore from a fresh backup instead. A memory that was in the trash in the backup is restored INTO the trash, and is counted in `imported_count` like the rest. Errors: `not_found` (no task with that id, or it belongs to another account, or it aged out after 7 days), `invalid_input` (the id is missing or not a string -- the schema layer answers this one).

If the user still needs to get a file INTO Amber, `amber_upload_backup` shows them an uploader; https://ambermem.com/backups documents the scripted route.

task_id.description: The id returned by whichever call started the restore: `amber_upload_backup` with action `finish`, `amber_import_memories`, or `POST /import/presign`. An unknown or expired id returns `code: not_found`.
The task this report is about.

status.description: `awaiting_upload` set up and waiting for the file, which is the normal state for the whole upload flow and NOT an error, `pending` queued, `running` restoring, `complete` finished, `failed` stopped (see `error`). A restore never sits on `running` for ever: a stall becomes `failed` with a reason.

imported_count.description: Memories PROCESSED so far, and the final count once status is `complete`. Not a fraction: the archive is never read in full up front, so nothing knows the total until the restore finishes. Not a count of new rows either: writes are keyed on the id the memory had in the archive, so restoring a file twice counts every memory again while writing none of them twice.

exported_at.description: When the archive was originally taken.

error.description: Why it stopped, when status is `failed`. Re-uploading the SAME file is safe and resumes rather than duplicating, so say that when you relay this.

tools.name: amber_delete_account
tools.title: Schedule account deletion
tools.description:
Schedule permanent account deletion in 30 days. Memory tools are blocked immediately (unlike cancellation, which keeps access until period end). Cancels the PayPal subscription. Reversible within 30 days via `amber_cancel_account_deletion`.

During the grace period: account management tools (status, export, feedback) remain accessible; memory tools are blocked. After 30 days: all data is permanently deleted.

Requires `confirm: true`. Returns `code: cancelled` when false, `code: already_scheduled` if already pending.

confirm.description: Set `true` to proceed, `false` to abort without changes. A STRINGIFIED boolean is also accepted (`"true"` and friends), because some clients JSON-stringify every argument; the published type is `boolean` because that is what a client should send.

status.description: Always `scheduled`: nothing is deleted at the moment of this call.

deletion_date.description: When the data will actually be destroyed (ISO 8601). Until then `amber_cancel_account_deletion` undoes this completely.

message.description: A human-readable summary. Relay it, including the date and the fact that it is reversible until then.

tools.name: amber_create_backup_key
tools.title: Create a backup key
tools.description:
Create a key that lets an automated job download a full export of this account without an AI session -- for example a weekly cron that saves everything to the user's own S3 bucket or NAS.

Usage: a backup is a task. `POST /backup` with header `X-Amber-Backup-Key: <key>` returns a `task_id`; poll `GET /backup/<task_id>` with the same header until `status` is `complete`, then download the `download_url` it carries. A ready-to-run weekly script is at https://ambermem.com/backups

IMPORTANT: the key is shown ONCE and never again -- only a hash is stored, so it cannot be recovered, only replaced. RELAY IT TO THE USER VERBATIM and tell them to save it somewhere safe.
There is one key per account: calling this again REPLACES the previous key, which immediately stops working. That is how rotation works, and how to respond if a key leaks. The response says when the replaced key was last used, so you can tell the user whether a scheduled job just stopped -- RELAY THAT WARNING if it is there, because the job will not report the failure itself.
The key does exactly TWO things: download an export, and start a restore -- which is a WRITE, so treat it as more than a read credential. It cannot read an individual memory, change the subscription, or delete the account. Corrected 2026-09-19: this said "exactly one thing ... cannot read, write or delete anything", which understated it, and the tool's own response text said the opposite. A restore also puts trashed memories back AS trash, which is a change rather than an addition. The backup includes deleted memories still in the trash.
Backups are limited to one per hour. Revoke with `amber_revoke_backup_key`. Not rate-limited.
ASK THE USER how long a gap without a successful backup should be treated as a problem, and pass it as `warn_after_days`. Without it Amber has to fall back to a cautious 30 days, and a backup that stopped is invisible until the day it is needed.

warn_after_days.description:
WARN THE USER WHEN NO BACKUP HAS SUCCEEDED FOR THIS MANY DAYS. It is the alert threshold itself, in days, used exactly as given: pass 10 and the warning appears once nothing has succeeded for 10 days. Nothing is multiplied or padded.

WHY IT EXISTS. A backup that stops does not announce itself. The job receives an error and writes it to a log nobody reads, so the user goes on believing they have backups and finds out on the day they need one, which is the only day it cannot be fixed. Amber can see WHEN a backup last succeeded and nothing else. It cannot know when the next one is due, whether the machine is meant to be on, or whether the user is on holiday. So the line between 'quiet' and 'broken' has to come from them.

HOW TO CHOOSE IT. Ask how often the job runs, then allow room for a missed run or two, and pass the RESULT. A nightly backup is comfortable at 3. The weekly script at the documented backup script is comfortable at 14 to 21. A monthly job wants 45 or more. Err high rather than low: a warning that fires on a healthy setup teaches the user to ignore the channel, and then the real one is ignored too.

DO NOT pass the backup interval itself. `warn_after_days: 7` for a weekly job means a single missed run raises a warning, which for most people is a machine that was off for a night.

WHEN AND WHERE IT FIRES. In the user's tool responses, at most once a day, and it clears itself the moment a backup succeeds again. There is nowhere else it can go: Amber holds no email address for anybody, by design. Relay it when you see it, because it is addressed to the user and they will not see it otherwise.

IT IS NOT THE ONLY CHECK. If something presents a backup key that was replaced or revoked, the user is told on their next message regardless of this number, and told what to fix. This threshold is the net that catches everything else: a dead machine, a disabled schedule, a full disk, an edited script.

IF YOU LEAVE IT OUT. Nothing breaks. An existing value is KEPT, so rotating a key does not silently widen the window. With no value at all Amber warns after 30 days. Prefer asking: for a nightly backup the default is a month of loss before anybody says anything.

CHANGING IT LATER means calling this tool again, which also REPLACES the key and forces the user to update their job. Ask now rather than revisiting it.

The backup-silence threshold now in force, in days: you are warned when no backup has succeeded for this many days. Echoed because creating a key is the only way to SET it, and a rotation that omits it deliberately carries the previous value forward -- so this is where you find out what you are on. Null means the server default applies.

backup_key.description: The key itself, shown ONCE and never recoverable. Relay it to the user verbatim and tell them to save it.

replaced_existing.description: True if this call revoked a previous key. Anything still using that key stops working immediately.

replaced_key_last_used_at.description: When the key this call just revoked was last used successfully, or null if it was never used (or there was none). NOT trivia: a recent timestamp means a scheduled job was relying on it and has just stopped, and that job will not report the failure itself. WARN THE USER when this is set.

example_command.description: A ready-to-run curl that starts a backup with this key. Safe to show.

message.description: A human-readable summary, including the replacement warning when there is one.

tools.name: amber_revoke_backup_key
tools.title: Revoke the backup key
tools.description: Revoke this account's backup key. Any automated job using it stops working immediately. Use this if a key may have leaked -- for example it was committed to a repository or pasted into a log. Returns `code: not_found` if no key exists. To rotate instead of simply revoking, call `amber_create_backup_key`, which replaces the old key in one step. Not rate-limited.

revoked.description: True if a key existed and is now revoked. False means there was nothing to revoke, which is reported as `code: not_found` rather than as success.

message.description: A human-readable summary of what happened.

tools.name: amber_cancel_account_deletion
tools.title: Cancel scheduled account deletion
tools.description:
Cancel a previously scheduled account deletion. Removes the deletion deadline and unblocks memory tools immediately. Access resumes until `next_billing_date` (the remaining paid period). No data is lost.

Side effects: clears `deletion_scheduled_at` from the account. The PayPal subscription was already cancelled when deletion was scheduled -- call `amber_reactivate_subscription` to start a new one if the paid period has expired. Returns `code: not_scheduled` if no deletion is pending. Not rate-limited.

status.description: Always `cancelled`: the scheduled deletion is off and the account is fully intact. Nothing had been destroyed while it was pending.

message.description: A human-readable confirmation to relay to the user.

tools.name: amber_send_feedback_to_developer
tools.title: Send feedback to the developer
tools.description: Send a structured bug report, feature request, or general feedback to Amber's developer. Send feedback PROACTIVELY when you encounter errors, unexpected behaviour, or the user expresses frustration -- briefly mention it to the user after sending, but do not ask for permission first. Never include passwords, API keys, or other sensitive personal information in any field. Rate-limited (bucket: 12 capacity, refills 1 per 5 minutes).

category.description: Determines how the developer triages this. 'bug': something broke or returned wrong results. 'feature_request': a capability that doesn't exist yet. 'usability': works but is confusing or awkward. 'general': anything else.

summary.description: One sentence, under 100 chars, and refused above 200. E.g. 'Search misses memories stored with emoji in content'.

details.description: Full reproduction context. Include: exact input used, expected outcome, actual outcome, any error codes. E.g. 'Stored "I love pizza 🍕" but searching "pizza emoji" returns nothing. Expected it to match.'

tool_context.description: The specific amber_ tool name involved, e.g. 'amber_search_memories'. Helps route the report.

status.description: Always `sent`: the report reached the developer. There is no reply channel, so do not promise the user an answer.

message.description: A human-readable confirmation to relay to the user.

tools.name: amber_mark_notification_read
tools.title: Mark a developer notification as read
tools.description:
Dismiss a developer notification after the user has acknowledged it. Permanently removes it from the `developer_notifications` block. That block is appended to a tool response ONLY WHEN there is at least one unread notification -- most responses will not contain it, and its absence means there is nothing pending, not that the feature is missing.

Side effects: deletes the notification row from the user's database. Idempotent in intent but returns `code: not_found` if already dismissed. Only call after the user has seen the notification content. Not rate-limited.

notification_id.description: Positive integer from the `id` field of a notification in `developer_notifications`. Example: if the block contains `{id: 42, message: "..."}`, pass 42. Each ID is unique and single-use.

status.description: Always `read`: the notification is acknowledged and will not be attached to further responses.

annotations.title: Mark a developer notification as read
